name: Solenoid Magnetic Field
description: Gives the magnetic flux density inside a long solenoid, B = μ0·n·i, where n is the number of turns per metre and i the current. The field is nearly uniform along the axis and independent of the radius.
notes: n must be turns per metre, not the total number of turns. This ideal-solenoid result assumes a long coil and ignores end effects near the openings.

name: Toroid Magnetic Field
description: Computes the magnetic field inside a toroid, B = μ0·N·i/(2·π·r), where N is the total number of turns and r the distance from the toroid axis. The field circulates within the ring and varies with r.
notes: N is the total turn count, and r is the mean radius at which the field is evaluated, not the coil cross-section radius. The field is essentially zero outside an ideal toroid.

name: Force Between Parallel Wires (per length)
description: Gives the force per unit length between two parallel current-carrying wires, μ0·i1·i2/(2·π·d), where d is their separation. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite currents repel.
notes: The result is a force per metre, not a total force; multiply by the wire length for the whole force. The sign of the effect depends on the relative current directions, which the magnitude formula does not capture.

name: Magnetic Field of Straight Wire
description: Computes the magnetic flux density at distance r from a long straight wire, B = μ0·i/(2·π·r). The field forms circles around the wire and falls off inversely with distance.
notes: This assumes an infinitely long, thin straight wire and gives the field only outside it. Distance in metres and current in amperes give the result in teslas.

name: Magnetic Field at Loop Centre
description: Gives the magnetic flux density at the centre of a single circular current loop, B = μ0·i/(2·r), where r is the loop radius. Smaller loops or larger currents give a stronger central field.
notes: This applies at the exact centre of a single turn; for N turns multiply by N. The field elsewhere along the axis is weaker and requires the full on-axis formula.

name: Magnetic Dipole Moment
description: Computes the magnetic dipole moment of a current loop, m = N·i·A, the product of the number of turns, the current, and the enclosed area. It sets the torque the loop feels in an external magnetic field.
notes: The area must be in square metres and is the area enclosed by one turn, not the wire cross-section. The moment is a vector normal to the loop; this gives only its magnitude.

name: Hall Voltage
description: Gives the Hall voltage across a conductor, i·b/(nq·q·t), that develops when current i flows through a sample of thickness t in a perpendicular magnetic field b. It reveals the sign and density of charge carriers.
notes: nq is the carrier number density per cubic metre and t is the sample dimension along the field. The magnetic field must be perpendicular to the current for this simple form to apply.

name: Lorentz Force on Moving Charge
description: Computes the magnetic force on a moving charge, F = q·v·b·sin θ, where θ is the angle between the velocity and the magnetic field. The force is maximal when motion is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel.
notes: The angle must be in radians. This is only the magnetic part of the Lorentz force; the force is always perpendicular to both velocity and field, so it does no work on the charge.

name: Larmor Radiated Power
description: Gives the power radiated by an accelerating point charge, P = q²·a²/(6·π·ε0·c³), from the Larmor formula. The radiated power grows with the square of the acceleration.
notes: This is the non-relativistic Larmor result; at speeds near c it needs the relativistic (Liénard) generalisation. Charge in coulombs and acceleration in metres per second squared give power in watts.

name: Poynting Vector Magnitude
description: Computes the magnitude of the Poynting vector, S = E·B/μ0, the instantaneous power per unit area carried by an electromagnetic wave with fields E and B. It points in the direction of energy flow.
notes: This uses instantaneous field values; for a sinusoidal wave the time-averaged intensity is half the peak value. E and B are the perpendicular field magnitudes and are related by E = c·B in vacuum.

name: Radiation Pressure (absorption)
description: Gives the radiation pressure exerted by light on a fully absorbing surface, p = I/c, where I is the incident intensity. For a perfectly reflecting surface the pressure would be twice as large.
notes: This form assumes complete absorption at normal incidence; reflection doubles it and oblique incidence reduces it. Intensity in watts per square metre gives pressure in pascals.

name: Ohm's law (V=IR)
description: Applies Ohm's law V=current×resistance to find the voltage across a resistor in volts, from current in amperes and resistance in ohms.
notes: Valid for ohmic (linear) conductors at constant temperature. Real components deviate when resistance changes with temperature or applied voltage.

name: Electric power (P=VI)
description: Computes electrical power as voltage×current, the rate of energy transfer in a circuit, in watts from voltage in volts and current in amperes.
notes: For DC or in-phase AC this gives real power. With AC where voltage and current are out of phase you must also include the power factor.

name: Power (P=I²R)
description: Computes power dissipated in a resistor as current²×resistance, in watts. This is the heat generated by a current flowing through a resistance.
notes: Current is squared, so doubling current quadruples the power. This form gives the power lost as heat in the resistance R.

name: Series resistance
description: Computes the total resistance of two resistors connected in series as r1+r2, in ohms. Resistances in series simply add together.
notes: Only valid for a series connection, where the same current flows through both. For parallel connection use the reciprocal formula instead.

name: Parallel resistance
description: Computes the combined resistance of two resistors in parallel as r1×r2÷(r1+r2), in ohms. The result is always smaller than either individual resistance.
notes: This product-over-sum form works for exactly two resistors. For three or more, use the reciprocal-sum formula 1/(1/r1+1/r2+…).

name: Ohm's law (voltage)
description: Applies Ohm's law to find the voltage across a resistor by multiplying the current through it by its resistance. With 2 A through 10 Ω the voltage is 20 V.
notes: Valid for ohmic (linear) resistors at constant temperature. Use amperes and ohms for a result in volts; the relationship breaks down for nonlinear or semiconductor devices.

name: Ohm's law (current)
description: Uses Ohm's law to find the current through a resistor by dividing the applied voltage by the resistance. Applying 12 V across 6 Ω drives a current of 2 A.
notes: Assumes an ohmic resistor at constant temperature. Enter volts and ohms for a result in amperes; resistance must be nonzero.

name: Ohm's law (resistance)
description: Rearranges Ohm's law to find resistance by dividing the voltage across a component by the current through it. A 12 V drop with 3 A of current corresponds to 4 Ω.
notes: Enter volts and amperes for a result in ohms. This gives the effective resistance at the operating point; for nonlinear elements it varies with current.

name: Power (P=V²/R)
description: Calculates the power dissipated in a resistor from the voltage across it and its resistance, as voltage squared divided by resistance. At 120 V across 60 Ω the power is 240 W.
notes: Voltage in volts and resistance in ohms give power in watts. Because voltage is squared, doubling the voltage quadruples the power; the voltage must be the value across that resistor.

name: Electrical energy
description: Computes the electrical energy consumed as the product of power and the time it is drawn. Running 100 W for 60 s uses 6000 J.
notes: Power in watts and time in seconds give energy in joules. Assumes constant power over the interval; for kilowatt-hours use power in kW and time in hours instead.

name: Electric charge (Q=It)
description: Finds the total electric charge that flows when a steady current runs for a given time, as current times time. A 2 A current for 30 s transfers 60 C.
notes: Current in amperes and time in seconds give charge in coulombs. Assumes a constant current; for a varying current the charge is the integral of current over time.

name: Capacitor charge (Q=CV)
description: Determines the charge stored on a capacitor as the product of its capacitance and the voltage across it. A 0.001 F capacitor at 12 V holds 0.012 C.
notes: Capacitance in farads and voltage in volts give charge in coulombs. Real capacitors are usually rated in µF or nF, so convert to farads before entering.

name: Energy in capacitor
description: Calculates the energy stored in a charged capacitor as half the capacitance times the voltage squared. A 0.001 F capacitor at 12 V stores 0.072 J.
notes: Capacitance in farads and voltage in volts give energy in joules. Because voltage is squared, energy rises steeply with voltage; equivalent forms are Q²/(2C) and QV/2.

name: Coulomb's law
description: Computes the electrostatic force between two point charges as Coulomb's constant times the product of the charges divided by the square of their separation. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
notes: Charges in coulombs and distance in meters give force in newtons. The result's sign follows the charge signs; the force weakens with the square of distance, so doubling separation quarters it.

name: Electric field (E=F/q)
description: Gives the electric field strength at a point as the force experienced by a test charge divided by that charge. A 0.05 N force on a 10⁻⁵ C charge means a field of 5000 N/C.
notes: Force in newtons and charge in coulombs give field in N/C (equal to V/m). Uses a small positive test charge; the field direction is that of the force on a positive charge.

name: Electric field (E=V/d)
description: Calculates the uniform electric field between two parallel plates as the voltage across them divided by their separation. With 100 V over 0.02 m the field is 5000 V/m.
notes: Voltage in volts and separation in meters give field in V/m (equal to N/C). Assumes a uniform field, valid for parallel plates ignoring edge effects.

name: Resistivity (R=ρL/A)
description: Finds the resistance of a uniform conductor from its material resistivity, length, and cross-sectional area. Resistance grows with length and falls with a larger cross-section.
notes: Use SI units: resistivity in Ω·m, length in meters, area in square meters, giving ohms. Resistivity is temperature dependent, so the value applies at its specified temperature.

name: Capacitors in series (two)
description: Computes the combined capacitance of two capacitors connected in series, as the reciprocal of the sum of their reciprocals. The total is always smaller than either individual capacitor.
notes: Enter both capacitances in the same unit (farads). In series capacitances add reciprocally, unlike resistors; the two capacitors also store the same charge.

name: Capacitors in parallel (two)
description: Gives the combined capacitance of two capacitors wired in parallel as the simple sum of their capacitances. The total exceeds either capacitor alone.
notes: Enter both capacitances in the same unit (farads). Parallel capacitors add directly, opposite to resistors, and share the same voltage across them.

name: LC resonant frequency
description: Calculates the natural resonant frequency of an inductor–capacitor circuit as 1/(2π√(LC)). At this frequency inductive and capacitive reactances cancel; larger L or C lowers the frequency.
notes: Inductance in henries and capacitance in farads give frequency in hertz. This ignores resistance; real circuits have damping that slightly shifts and broadens the resonance.

name: Inductive reactance
description: Finds the opposition an inductor presents to alternating current as 2π times frequency times inductance. Reactance rises with frequency, so inductors impede high-frequency signals more.
notes: Frequency in hertz and inductance in henries give reactance in ohms. Reactance stores and returns energy rather than dissipating it, and it is zero at DC.

name: Capacitive reactance
description: Computes the opposition a capacitor presents to alternating current as 1/(2π·frequency·capacitance). Reactance falls as frequency rises, so capacitors pass high-frequency signals more easily.
notes: Frequency in hertz and capacitance in farads give reactance in ohms. It approaches infinity at DC (blocking direct current) and does not dissipate energy.

name: Transformer secondary voltage
description: Calculates a transformer's secondary voltage from the primary voltage scaled by the ratio of secondary to primary turns. More secondary turns step the voltage up, fewer step it down.
notes: The turns count units cancel, so only their ratio matters. Assumes an ideal transformer with no losses; real transformers deliver slightly less due to winding resistance and leakage.

name: Magnetic force on charge
description: Computes the magnetic (Lorentz) force on a moving charge as charge times velocity times field strength times the sine of the angle between velocity and field. The force is maximal when motion is perpendicular to the field.
notes: The angle is in radians between velocity and field; at 0 (parallel) the force vanishes. This gives magnitude only, and the force acts perpendicular to both velocity and field.

name: Force on current-carrying wire
description: Finds the magnetic force on a straight current-carrying wire in a field as field times current times length times the sine of the angle between the wire and the field. It peaks when the wire is perpendicular to the field.
notes: The angle is in radians; a wire parallel to the field (angle 0) feels no force. Assumes a uniform field and a straight wire, and gives magnitude only.

name: Energy in inductor
description: Calculates the energy stored in an inductor's magnetic field as half the inductance times the current squared. A 0.5 H inductor carrying 2 A stores 1 J.
notes: Inductance in henries and current in amperes give energy in joules. Because current is squared, energy grows steeply with current; the energy is held in the magnetic field while current flows.

name: Parallel-plate capacitance
description: Calculates the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor as the permittivity times the plate area divided by the gap between plates. Larger plates or a smaller gap increase capacitance.
notes: Use SI units: permittivity in F/m, area in m², separation in meters, giving farads. Use the material's permittivity (ε₀ times relative permittivity) and neglect fringing at the edges.

name: Drift velocity
description: Finds the average drift velocity of charge carriers in a conductor from the current, carrier number density, cross-sectional area, and charge per carrier. Drift speeds are typically very slow, well under a millimeter per second.
notes: Use SI units: current in A, density in 1/m³, area in m², charge in coulombs, giving m/s. Drift velocity is far slower than the near-light-speed propagation of the electrical signal itself.

name: RC time constant
description: Computes the time constant of a resistor–capacitor circuit as the product of resistance and capacitance. It is the time for the capacitor voltage to reach about 63% of its final value while charging.
notes: Resistance in ohms and capacitance in farads give seconds. After about five time constants the capacitor is regarded as fully charged or discharged.

name: RL time constant
description: Calculates the time constant of a resistor–inductor circuit as inductance divided by resistance. It is the time for the current to reach about 63% of its final value as it builds up.
notes: Inductance in henries and resistance in ohms give seconds. After roughly five time constants the current is treated as having reached its steady value.

name: Magnetic flux
description: Computes the magnetic flux through a flat surface as field strength times area times the cosine of the angle between the field and the surface normal. Flux is maximal when the field is perpendicular to the surface.
notes: Field in teslas and area in m² give webers. The angle is measured from the surface normal in radians, so 0 gives maximum flux and π/2 gives zero.

name: Induced EMF (Faraday)
description: Estimates the average induced electromotive force in a coil from Faraday's law, as the number of turns times the flux change divided by the time interval. Faster flux change or more turns produce a larger EMF.
notes: Flux change in webers and time in seconds give volts. This gives the average magnitude; the actual EMF opposes the change (Lenz's law), so it carries a negative sign in the full form.

name: Cyclotron frequency
description: Finds the orbital frequency of a charged particle circling in a magnetic field as charge times field divided by 2π times mass. It depends only on the charge-to-mass ratio and field, not on speed.
notes: Use SI units: charge in coulombs, field in teslas, mass in kilograms, giving hertz. This is the non-relativistic value; at speeds near light the effective mass increases and the frequency drops.

name: Voltage divider
description: Calculates the output voltage of a two-resistor voltage divider as the input voltage times the ratio of the lower resistor to the sum of both resistors. Here 12 V across 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ yields 8 V across R2.
notes: Both resistances in the same unit; the output is taken across R2. Assumes negligible load current; a real load draws current and lowers the output below this ideal value.

name: Energy from charge and voltage
description: Computes the energy transferred when a charge moves through a potential difference, as charge times voltage. Moving 0.005 C through 12 V transfers 0.06 J.
notes: Charge in coulombs and voltage in volts give joules. This assumes a fixed voltage; for charging a capacitor from zero the stored energy is only half of QV.

name: Current divider
description: Finds the current through one branch of two parallel resistors as the total current times the ratio of the opposite resistor to the sum of both. The larger share of current flows through the smaller resistor.
notes: Both resistances in the same unit; note this branch's current uses the other resistor (R2) in the numerator. Applies to two resistors in parallel carrying a shared total current.

name: AC RMS Voltage from Peak
description: Converts the peak amplitude of a sinusoidal AC voltage to its root-mean-square (RMS) value, as peak voltage divided by the square root of two. The RMS value in volts is the equivalent DC voltage delivering the same average power.
notes: Valid only for a pure sinusoidal waveform; non-sinusoidal signals have a different peak-to-RMS ratio. Do not confuse peak with peak-to-peak, which is twice the peak.

name: AC Average (Rectified) Voltage
description: Computes the average value of a full-wave rectified sinusoidal voltage over a half cycle, as two times peak voltage divided by pi. The result in volts is the mean absolute voltage, about 0.637 times the peak.
notes: This is the rectified average, not the RMS value, and applies to a pure sine wave. The average of an unrectified sinusoid over a full cycle is zero, so rectification is assumed.

name: Real (Active) Power
description: Calculates the real (active) power consumed in an AC circuit, as RMS voltage times RMS current times the cosine of the phase angle. The result in watts is the power actually converted to useful work or heat.
notes: Voltage and current must be RMS values and the phase angle in radians. Real power is always less than or equal to apparent power, being equal only at unity power factor.

name: Apparent Power
description: Computes the apparent power in an AC circuit as the product of RMS voltage and RMS current. The result in volt-amperes is the total power that appears to flow, combining real and reactive components.
notes: Apparent power is measured in VA, not watts, and equals the magnitude of the complex power. It equals real power only when the power factor is 1 (purely resistive load).

name: Reactive Power
description: Calculates the reactive power in an AC circuit, as RMS voltage times RMS current times the sine of the phase angle. The result in volt-amperes reactive is the power that oscillates between source and reactive loads without doing net work.
notes: Voltage and current are RMS and the phase angle is in radians. Reactive power is positive for inductive loads and negative for capacitive loads; it does no net average work.

name: Series RLC Quality Factor
description: Computes the quality factor Q of a series RLC circuit as (1/R)*sqrt(L/C). It is a dimensionless measure of resonance sharpness: higher Q means lower energy loss per cycle and a narrower, more selective resonance peak.
notes: Valid for a series RLC circuit where R is the total series resistance. Q is dimensionless, so use SI units (ohms, henries, farads) consistently. Series and parallel circuits use different Q formulas.

name: Resonant Bandwidth
description: Gives the -3 dB bandwidth of a resonant circuit as the resonant frequency f0 divided by the quality factor Q. The result, in hertz, is the width of the frequency band over which the circuit responds strongly.
notes: Q must be dimensionless and f0 in hertz, giving bandwidth in hertz. Higher Q yields a narrower bandwidth. This is the half-power (-3 dB) width, not the full frequency span.

name: Skin Depth
description: Calculates the skin depth of an alternating current in a conductor, sqrt(rho/(pi*f*mu)), the depth at which current density falls to 1/e of its surface value. It shows how AC concentrates near the conductor surface as frequency rises.
notes: Permeability mu is the absolute value (mu0 times relative permeability), not just mu0. Skin depth decreases with higher frequency and higher permeability. Assumes a good conductor and uniform material.

name: Capacitor Energy Density
description: Computes the electric-field energy density 0.5*eps*E^2 stored in a dielectric, in joules per cubic meter. It gives the energy per unit volume held in an electric field of strength E within a medium of permittivity eps.
notes: Permittivity eps is the absolute permittivity (eps0 times relative permittivity) of the dielectric, not eps0 alone. Energy density grows with the square of the field, so doubling E quadruples the stored energy.

name: Magnetic Energy Density
description: Computes the magnetic energy density B^2/(2*mu0) stored in a magnetic field, in joules per cubic meter. It gives the energy per unit volume held in a field of flux density B within a medium of permeability mu0.
notes: Use the absolute permeability of the medium; for vacuum or air mu0 is about 1.2566e-6 T·m/A. Energy density scales with the square of B, so doubling the flux density quadruples the energy.

name: RLC Impedance Magnitude
description: Computes the magnitude of the impedance of a series RLC circuit as sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2), in ohms. It combines resistance with the net reactance (inductive minus capacitive) to give the total opposition to AC current.
notes: XL and XC are the reactance magnitudes at the operating frequency; the formula uses their difference. At resonance XL equals XC, so the impedance reduces to R. This gives magnitude only, not phase.

name: Three-Phase Real Power
description: Computes the real (active) power delivered by a balanced three-phase system from line voltage V, line current I, and the phase angle φ between voltage and current, using P = √3·V·I·cos(φ).
notes: φ is entered in degrees and converted internally to radians; V and I are line (not phase) quantities, and cos(φ) is the power factor.

name: Power Factor
description: Computes the power factor of an AC circuit as the ratio of real (active) power P to apparent power S, PF = P/S, a dimensionless value between 0 and 1.
notes: A power factor of 1 means all supplied power does real work; lower values indicate more reactive power relative to real power. P and S must be in consistent units (W and VA).

name: Apparent Power from Active and Reactive Power
description: Computes the apparent power S of an AC circuit from its real power P and reactive power Q using the power triangle relationship S = √(P²+Q²).
notes: P, Q, and S form a right triangle (the power triangle); enter P and Q in the same numeric scale (e.g., both in W/var, or both in kW/kvar) so S comes out in matching VA.

name: Voltage Drop (Feeder/Cable)
description: Estimates the voltage drop along a single-phase two-wire feeder or cable run from the load current I, the cable's resistance R and reactance X per conductor, and the power-factor angle θ, using the simplified approximate formula e = 2I(Rcosθ + Xsinθ).
notes: θ is entered in degrees (the angle whose cosine is the load power factor) and converted internally to radians. The factor of 2 accounts for the outgoing and return conductors; R and X should already be per-conductor totals for the full run length.

name: Power-Factor Correction Capacitor Size
description: Sizes the reactive power (capacitor bank rating) needed to raise a load's power factor from an original value pf1 to a higher target value pf2, using Qc = P×(tan(cos⁻¹(pf1)) − tan(cos⁻¹(pf2))).
notes: pf1 and pf2 are entered as decimals (e.g., 0.75), not percentages, and pf2 must be greater than pf1 for a positive, sensible capacitor size. The result shares whatever power unit P is given in (e.g., kW in → kvar out).

name: Joule Heat (with Time)
description: Computes the heat energy Q dissipated by a resistor carrying current I for a duration t, using Joule's law Q = I²Rt.
notes: t must be in seconds for the result to come out in joules; for time given in hours or minutes, convert first (or divide the joule result by 3600 to get Wh).

name: Transformer Efficiency
description: Computes a transformer's efficiency as a percentage from its output power and total losses (copper + core losses), using η = Pout/(Pout+losses)×100, since input power equals output power plus losses.
notes: pout and losses must be in the same power unit. Typical power transformers run in the high-90s percent; a low result usually means losses are large relative to the load.

name: Synchronous Speed (AC Motor/Generator)
description: Computes the synchronous speed of an AC induction motor or synchronous generator from the supply frequency f and the number of magnetic poles p, using Ns = 120×f/p.
notes: p is the total pole count (always an even number, e.g., 2, 4, 6), not the number of pole pairs. The actual rotor speed of an induction motor runs slightly below this synchronous speed due to slip.

name: Speed of a Charged Particle Accelerated Through a Potential Difference
description: Calculates the final speed gained by a charged particle starting from rest as it is accelerated through a given potential difference (voltage). It follows from equating the electric potential energy lost to the kinetic energy gained.
notes: Non-relativistic approximation; becomes inaccurate when the resulting speed approaches a significant fraction of the speed of light (roughly above 10% of c, i.e. very high accelerating voltages for light particles like electrons).

name: Deflection of a Charged Particle in a Uniform Electric Field (Parallel Plates)
description: Calculates the transverse (perpendicular) deflection of a charged particle as it travels at constant horizontal speed through a uniform electric field between parallel plates, such as in a cathode ray tube or velocity selector. It treats the motion as projectile-like, with constant horizontal velocity and constant transverse acceleration from the field.
notes: Assumes the deflection is small compared with the plate separation (so the particle does not strike a plate before exiting) and that fringing fields at the plate edges are negligible.

name: Coulomb Potential Energy of Two Charges
description: Computes the electrostatic potential energy stored by two point charges q1 and q2 separated by distance r, using Coulomb constant 8.99e9. Like charges give positive energy (repulsion), opposite charges give negative energy (attraction).
notes: Charges must be in coulombs and r in metres. The sign of the result carries physical meaning; energy diverges as r approaches zero and vanishes at infinite separation.

name: Electric Field of a Dipole (Axial)
description: Gives the electric field strength along the axis of an electric dipole with dipole moment p at distance r, as 2×8.99e9×p/r³. The field points along the dipole axis and falls off with the cube of distance.
notes: Valid only in the far field where r is much larger than the charge separation. The axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance.

name: Electric Field of a Dipole (Equatorial)
description: Gives the electric field strength on the equatorial (perpendicular bisector) plane of an electric dipole with moment p at distance r, as 8.99e9×p/r³. The field is antiparallel to the dipole moment.
notes: Valid only in the far field where r greatly exceeds the charge separation. This equatorial field is half the axial field at the same distance.

name: Torque on an Electric Dipole
description: Computes the torque p×Ef×sin(theta) that a uniform electric field Ef exerts on an electric dipole of moment p, where theta is the angle between the dipole and the field. The torque tends to align the dipole with the field.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. Torque is zero when the dipole is aligned (theta=0) or anti-aligned (theta=pi) and maximal at 90 degrees.

name: Potential Energy of an Electric Dipole
description: Computes the potential energy -p×Ef×cos(theta) of an electric dipole of moment p in a uniform field Ef, where theta is the angle between them. Energy is lowest when aligned with the field and highest when opposed.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. The result is negative for theta below 90 degrees (favourable alignment) and positive above it; only energy differences are physically meaningful.

name: Spherical Capacitor Capacitance
description: Computes the capacitance of a spherical capacitor formed by two concentric conducting shells of inner radius r1 and outer radius r2, as 4×pi×eps0×r1×r2/(r2-r1). Capacitance grows as the gap between shells shrinks.
notes: Requires r2 greater than r1, both in metres. Assumes vacuum between the shells; for a dielectric, replace 8.85e-12 with the medium permittivity.

name: Cylindrical Capacitor Capacitance
description: Computes the capacitance of a cylindrical capacitor of length L with inner radius r1 and outer radius r2, as 2×pi×eps0×L/ln(r2/r1). It models coaxial conductors and grows with length.
notes: Requires r2 greater than r1 and uses the natural log. Assumes a long cylinder so edge effects are neglected; vacuum dielectric is assumed via 8.85e-12.

name: Capacitance of an Isolated Sphere
description: Computes the self-capacitance of an isolated conducting sphere of radius R in vacuum, as 4×pi×eps0×R. It measures how much charge the sphere holds per volt relative to infinity.
notes: Radius R is in metres and the result scales linearly with R. Assumes vacuum surroundings; nearby conductors would change the effective capacitance.

name: Electric Field Energy Density
description: Computes the energy stored per unit volume in an electric field, as 0.5×eps0×Ef², where Ef is the field strength in vacuum. It quantifies how much energy is packed into the field itself.
notes: Field Ef is in volts per metre and the result is in joules per cubic metre. Uses vacuum permittivity; in a dielectric replace 8.85e-12 with the medium value.

name: Coaxial Cable Inductance per Length
description: Computes the external inductance per unit length of a coaxial cable with inner conductor radius a and outer conductor radius b, as (mu0/2pi)×ln(b/a). It gives inductance in henries per metre.
notes: Requires b greater than a and uses the natural log. This is the external inductance only, neglecting the internal contribution of the conductors; a vacuum-like permeability is assumed.

name: Electric Field of an Infinite Line Charge
description: Computes the radial electric field at distance r from an infinite straight line of charge with linear charge density lambda, as lambda/(2×pi×eps0×r). The field points away from the line and falls off as 1/r.
notes: Distance r is the perpendicular distance in metres and lambda is charge per metre. Valid only for an idealized infinite line; near the ends of a finite wire it overestimates the field.

name: Electric Field of an Infinite Charged Plane
description: Computes the electric field produced by an infinite plane with uniform surface charge density sigma, as sigma/(2×eps0). The field is uniform, points away from the plane, and is independent of distance.
notes: Surface charge sigma is in coulombs per square metre. The result is per single sheet; for a conductor surface or between capacitor plates the field is instead sigma/eps0.

name: Field Inside a Uniformly Charged Sphere
description: Computes the electric field at radius r inside a uniformly charged sphere of total charge Q and radius R, as 8.99e9×Q×r/R³. The field grows linearly from zero at the centre to the surface value.
notes: Valid only for r less than or equal to R and for uniform volume charge. Outside the sphere the field instead follows the inverse-square law 8.99e9×Q/r².

name: On-Axis Magnetic Field of a Circular Loop
description: Computes the magnetic flux density on the axis of a circular current loop of radius R carrying current I, at axial distance x, as mu0×I×R²/(2×(R²+x²)^1.5). It peaks at the loop centre and decays along the axis.
notes: Valid only on the loop axis; off-axis points require a fuller treatment. Setting x=0 recovers the well-known centre field mu0×I/(2R).

name: Helmholtz Coil Central Field
description: Computes the highly uniform magnetic field at the centre of a Helmholtz coil pair, each with N turns of radius R carrying current I, as 8×mu0×N×I/(5×sqrt(5)×R). This is the standard formula for the coil midpoint.
notes: Assumes the two coils are separated by exactly one radius R, which gives the uniform central region. N is turns per single coil, not both combined.

name: Force per Length Between Parallel Wires
description: Computes the magnetic force per unit length between two long parallel wires carrying currents I1 and I2 separated by distance d, as mu0×I1×I2/(2×pi×d). Currents in the same direction attract, opposite directions repel.
notes: Separation d is in metres and the result is force per metre. Assumes long, thin, parallel wires; the sign of the interaction depends on the relative current directions.

name: Hall Coefficient
description: Computes the Hall coefficient 1/(n×q) of a conductor with carrier density n and carrier charge q. It relates the transverse Hall voltage to the current and magnetic field and reveals the carrier sign and density.
notes: Carrier density n is per cubic metre and q is the carrier charge in coulombs. The sign follows the carrier charge, so it is negative for electrons and positive for holes.

name: Curie's Law Susceptibility
description: Computes the magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnet by Curie's law, C/T, where C is the Curie constant and T the absolute temperature. Susceptibility rises as the material is cooled.
notes: Temperature T must be in kelvin. Curie's law holds only for ideal paramagnets at high temperature and weak fields; it breaks down near magnetic ordering transitions.

name: Reluctance of a Magnetic Circuit
description: Computes the magnetic reluctance l/(mu×A) of a flux path of length l, permeability mu, and cross-sectional area A. Reluctance is the magnetic analogue of resistance, opposing magnetic flux.
notes: Length l is in metres, area A in square metres, and mu is the absolute permeability. Assumes uniform cross-section and no flux leakage or fringing.

name: Energy Stored in an Inductor
description: Computes the energy stored in the magnetic field of an inductor of inductance L carrying current I, as 0.5×L×I². The energy grows with the square of the current.
notes: Inductance L is in henries and current I in amperes. Assumes a constant inductance; in saturable magnetic cores L varies with current and the formula becomes approximate.

name: Mutual Inductance of Coaxial Solenoids
description: Computes the mutual inductance between two coaxial solenoids with N1 and N2 turns sharing cross-section A over length l, as mu0×N1×N2×A/l. It measures the flux linkage from one coil to the other.
notes: Assumes tightly wound, long solenoids with full flux coupling and equal length l. Real coils with leakage flux have a somewhat smaller mutual inductance.

name: Self-Inductance of a Solenoid
description: Computes the self-inductance of a solenoid with N turns, cross-sectional area A, and length l, as mu0×N²×A/l. Inductance grows with the square of the turn count.
notes: Assumes a long, tightly wound air-core solenoid so end effects are negligible. For a magnetic core, replace 1.2566e-6 with the core permeability.

name: Self-Inductance of a Toroid
description: Computes the self-inductance of a rectangular-cross-section toroid with N turns, height h, inner radius a, and outer radius b, as mu0×N²×h×ln(b/a)/(2×pi). It accounts for the varying field across the toroid.
notes: Requires b greater than a and uses the natural log. Assumes an air core and uniform winding; a magnetic core replaces 1.2566e-6 with its permeability.

name: Radiation Pressure (Total Reflection)
description: Computes the radiation pressure exerted by light of intensity S on a perfectly reflecting surface, as 2×S/c with c the speed of light. Reflection doubles the pressure compared to full absorption.
notes: Intensity S is in watts per square metre and assumes normal incidence on a perfect reflector. For a fully absorbing surface the pressure is instead S/c.

name: Wave Speed in a Dielectric Medium
description: Computes the speed of an electromagnetic wave in a medium of permeability mu and permittivity eps, as 1/sqrt(mu×eps). In vacuum this reduces to the speed of light.
notes: Uses absolute (not relative) permeability and permittivity in SI units. The result cannot exceed the vacuum speed of light for ordinary passive media.

name: Fresnel Reflectance at Normal Incidence
description: Computes the fraction of light power reflected at normal incidence between two media with refractive indices n1 and n2, as ((n1-n2)/(n1+n2))². It gives the reflectance for an ideal flat interface.
notes: Valid only at normal incidence and for non-absorbing media; the result is a fraction between 0 and 1. Transmittance is one minus this value.

name: Refractive Index from Permittivity
description: Computes the refractive index of a medium from its relative permittivity er and relative permeability mur, as sqrt(er×mur). For most non-magnetic materials mur is close to 1.
notes: Both inputs are dimensionless relative quantities. Assumes lossless, non-dispersive media; at optical frequencies er often differs from its static value.

name: Electric Susceptibility from Permittivity
description: Computes the electric susceptibility of a dielectric from its relative permittivity er, as er-1. Susceptibility measures how readily the material polarizes in an applied electric field.
notes: Relative permittivity er is dimensionless and at least 1 for ordinary dielectrics, giving a non-negative susceptibility. Vacuum (er=1) has zero susceptibility.

name: Motional EMF of a Sliding Rod
description: Computes the motional EMF B×L×v induced across a rod of length L moving at velocity v perpendicular to a magnetic field B. It is the voltage generated by the changing area of the circuit.
notes: Assumes B, the rod, and the velocity are mutually perpendicular; otherwise the relevant components must be used. Field B is in tesla and velocity in metres per second.

name: Peak EMF of a Rotating Coil
description: Computes the peak EMF N×B×A×omega of a coil with N turns and area A rotating at angular speed omega in a magnetic field B. This is the amplitude of the sinusoidal AC voltage from a generator.
notes: Angular speed omega is in radians per second and this gives the peak, not RMS, value. The RMS voltage is this result divided by sqrt(2).

name: Magnetic Pressure
description: Computes the magnetic pressure B²/(2×mu0) associated with a magnetic field of strength B, equal to the energy density of the field. It represents the outward push a magnetic field can exert.
notes: Field B is in tesla and the result is in pascals, using vacuum permeability. This equals the magnetic energy density and is numerically important in plasma and fusion contexts.

name: Potential Energy of a Magnetic Dipole
description: Computes the potential energy -m×B×cos(theta) of a magnetic dipole of moment m in a field B, where theta is the angle between them. Energy is minimal when aligned with the field.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. The result is negative for favourable alignment (theta below 90 degrees); only energy differences carry physical meaning.

name: Torque on a Magnetic Dipole
description: Computes the torque m×B×sin(theta) that a magnetic field B exerts on a magnetic dipole of moment m, where theta is the angle between them. The torque tends to align the dipole with the field.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. Torque vanishes when aligned (theta=0) or anti-aligned (theta=pi) and is largest at 90 degrees.

name: Debye Screening Length
description: Computes the Debye screening length sqrt(eps0×kB×T/(n×q²)) over which electric fields are screened in a plasma of temperature T, number density n, and charge q. Beyond it, charges are effectively shielded.
notes: Temperature T is in kelvin and n in particles per cubic metre. The formula assumes a classical, quasi-neutral plasma with many particles within the Debye sphere.

name: Plasma Frequency
description: Computes the electron plasma frequency sqrt(n×q²/(eps0×mass))/(2×pi) in hertz for a plasma of electron density n. It is the natural oscillation frequency of the electron gas about the ions.
notes: Density n is per cubic metre and mass is the electron mass. Dividing by 2pi gives frequency in hertz rather than angular frequency; electromagnetic waves below it cannot propagate.

name: Cyclotron Radius (Gyroradius)
description: Computes the radius mass×v/(q×B) of the circular orbit of a charged particle moving at speed v perpendicular to a magnetic field B. It is the gyroradius of the particle's helical motion.
notes: Speed v should be the component perpendicular to B. This is the non-relativistic form; at relativistic speeds mass must be replaced by the relativistic mass.

name: E×B Drift Velocity
description: Computes the E×B drift speed Ef/B of a charged particle in crossed electric field Ef and magnetic field B. Remarkably, this drift is independent of the particle's charge and mass.
notes: Assumes Ef and B are perpendicular; the drift direction is along E×B. Field Ef is in volts per metre and B in tesla, giving the drift speed in metres per second.

name: Alfvén Speed
description: Computes the Alfvén speed B/sqrt(mu0×rho) at which magnetic disturbances travel through a plasma of mass density rho in a magnetic field B. It sets the pace of magnetohydrodynamic waves.
notes: Field B is in tesla and mass density rho in kilograms per cubic metre, using vacuum permeability. Valid in the ideal MHD regime of a magnetized plasma.

name: Larmor Precession Frequency
description: Computes the Larmor precession frequency gamma×B/(2×pi) in hertz at which a magnetic moment precesses about a magnetic field B, given the gyromagnetic ratio gamma. It underlies NMR and MRI.
notes: The gyromagnetic ratio gamma here is in radians per second per tesla, and dividing by 2pi yields frequency in hertz rather than angular frequency.

name: Electric Polarization Density
description: Computes the electric polarization density eps0×chi×Ef of a linear dielectric with susceptibility chi in an applied field Ef. It is the induced dipole moment per unit volume.
notes: Susceptibility chi is dimensionless and field Ef is in volts per metre, giving polarization in coulombs per square metre. Valid only for linear, isotropic dielectrics.

name: Displacement Current (Parallel Plate)
description: Computes the displacement current eps0×A×dEdt in a parallel-plate capacitor of plate area A when the electric field changes at rate dEdt. It behaves as a current that sustains the magnetic field between the plates.
notes: Plate area A is in square metres and dEdt is the rate of change of the field in volts per metre per second. Assumes a uniform field and vacuum dielectric.

name: Electric Field of a Point Charge
description: Computes the electric field strength produced by a point charge Q at distance r, as k×Q/r² with Coulomb's constant k=8.99e9. The field points radially away from a positive charge and falls off with the square of distance.
notes: Charge Q is in coulombs and r in metres; r must be nonzero. Assumes a vacuum (or air) and an idealized point charge.

name: Parallel Plate Capacitor Capacitance
description: Computes the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with plate area A and separation d, as eps0×A/d using vacuum permittivity 8.85e-12. Capacitance grows with plate area and shrinks as the gap widens.
notes: Plate area A is in square metres and separation d in metres. Assumes a vacuum (or air) dielectric and neglects fringing fields; for an inserted dielectric multiply by its relative permittivity.

name: Magnetomotive Force
description: Computes the magnetomotive force (MMF) driving flux around a magnetic circuit, as the number of coil turns N times the current I. It is the magnetic analogue of EMF in an electric circuit.
notes: N is a plain turn count and I is in amperes; the result is in ampere-turns. Pairs with the reluctance of the circuit to give the resulting flux via MMF = flux × reluctance.

name: Flux Density from Field Strength
description: Computes the magnetic flux density B produced in a material of permeability mu subjected to field strength H, as B=mu×H. It links the applied field to the resulting flux density in that medium.
notes: Use the absolute permeability mu (H/m), not a relative value; for free space enter 1.2566e-6, and for a magnetic core use mu0 times the material's relative permeability. Field strength H is in amperes per metre.

name: Electric Potential Due to a Point Charge
description: Calculates the electric potential at a distance from an idealized point charge, taking the potential at infinity as zero. It uses Coulomb's constant to relate the potential directly to the charge and distance.
notes: Assumes a point charge (or a spherically symmetric charge distribution, measured outside it) in vacuum or air, and that r is measured from the center of the charge.
